questions.body: What exception is thrown when a thread that is sleeping or waiting via `Thread.sleep()` or `Object.wait()` has its `interrupt()` method called by another thread?
questions.keyPoints: InterruptedException is thrown when an interrupted thread is in a blocking state like sleep(), wait(), or join().

options.text: InterruptedException
options.explanation: Methods that block such as Thread.sleep(), Object.wait(), and Thread.join() declare and throw checked InterruptedException when interrupted.

options.text: IllegalThreadStateException
options.explanation: IllegalThreadStateException is thrown when attempting an invalid state transition, such as restarting an already terminated or running thread.

options.text: TimeoutException
options.explanation: TimeoutException is used in Future.get(timeout) when an operation exceeds its allotted time limit.

options.text: ThreadDeath
options.explanation: ThreadDeath is an error thrown when the deprecated Thread.stop() method is invoked.

questions.body: What is the primary difference between `java.lang.Runnable` and `java.util.concurrent.Callable<V>` in Java?
questions.keyPoints: Callable can return a value and throw checked exceptions; Runnable returns void and cannot throw checked exceptions.

options.text: Callable's call() method can return a typed result and throw checked exceptions, whereas Runnable's run() returns void and cannot throw checked exceptions.
options.explanation: Callable<V> defines 'V call() throws Exception', allowing both return values and checked exceptions, unlike Runnable's 'void run()'.

options.text: Runnable can only be executed by raw Thread instances, while Callable can only be executed in a ForkJoinPool.
options.explanation: Both Runnable and Callable can be executed or submitted to ExecutorService thread pools.

options.text: Callable runs on an asynchronous daemon thread, while Runnable always runs synchronously on the main thread.
options.explanation: Both execute on whichever thread they are dispatched to; daemon status depends on the thread factory.

options.text: Runnable is thread-safe by default, whereas Callable requires manual synchronized blocks.
options.explanation: Neither interface guarantees thread-safety of shared state by default.

questions.body: When a thread executes a `synchronized static` method in class `OrderService`, which intrinsic lock (monitor) does it acquire?
questions.keyPoints: Static synchronized methods acquire the monitor lock on the java.lang.Class object of the class.

options.text: The Class object monitor lock: OrderService.class
options.explanation: Static synchronized methods synchronize on the Class object representing that class, rather than an instance of the class.

options.text: The current instance monitor lock: this
options.explanation: 'this' does not exist in a static context; instance synchronized methods synchronize on 'this'.

options.text: The JVM's global thread group monitor lock
options.explanation: There is no global thread group monitor lock used for static method synchronization.

options.text: The Thread.currentThread() lock
options.explanation: The current thread is the lock holder, not the lock monitor object.

questions.body: What guarantees does the `volatile` modifier provide for a shared variable in Java?
questions.keyPoints: Volatile guarantees visibility across threads and prevents instruction reordering (happens-before), but does NOT guarantee atomicity of compound operations.

options.text: Visibility of changes across threads and ordering (prevents reordering), but does not guarantee atomicity of compound operations like increment (count++).
options.explanation: Volatile establishes a happens-before relationship ensuring all writes are immediately visible to subsequent reads, but compound operations like count++ (read-modify-write) are non-atomic.

options.text: Complete mutual exclusion and atomicity for all operations performed on the variable.
options.explanation: Mutual exclusion requires locks or synchronized blocks; volatile alone is not sufficient for compound actions.

options.text: Prevents garbage collection of the referenced object as long as any thread is alive.
options.explanation: Volatile has no effect on GC reachability rules.

options.text: Forces the variable to be allocated in thread-local CPU register memory.
options.explanation: Volatile forces reads/writes directly to main memory (or flushed through CPU cache coherency), avoiding stale CPU cache/register values.

questions.body: How do classes in `java.util.concurrent.atomic` (like `AtomicInteger`) achieve thread-safety without using traditional `synchronized` locks?
questions.keyPoints: Atomic classes use hardware-level Compare-And-Swap (CAS) instructions for lock-free thread safety.

options.text: They use low-level CPU Compare-And-Swap (CAS) instructions via VarHandle / Unsafe in a lock-free optimistic retry loop.
options.explanation: Atomic variables rely on hardware CAS primitive operations (compareAndSet) to atomically update values without thread blocking or kernel context switching.

options.text: They create a deep clone of the value inside a ThreadLocal variable for every thread.
options.explanation: ThreadLocal keeps per-thread isolated copies, whereas AtomicInteger shares one mutable value safely across threads.

options.text: They suspend the JVM execution pipeline during each arithmetic write.
options.explanation: The JVM is not suspended; CAS executes at the CPU instruction level.

options.text: They wrap all method calls in an OS-level sem_wait system call.
options.explanation: OS semaphores are blocking kernel constructs; CAS is a non-blocking user-space CPU instruction.

questions.body: Why must `object.wait()`, `object.notify()`, and `object.notifyAll()` always be called from within a `synchronized` block on that specific object?
questions.keyPoints: Calling wait() or notify() without holding the monitor lock throws IllegalMonitorStateException and causes race conditions.

options.text: To prevent lost-wakeups and race conditions between testing a condition and going to sleep; otherwise, an IllegalMonitorStateException is thrown.
options.explanation: The calling thread must own the monitor lock to inspect state predicates and sleep atomically, preventing missed notify signals. The JVM throws IllegalMonitorStateException if unowned.

options.text: Because wait() allocates new heap memory that requires synchronized GC barriers.
options.explanation: wait() releases the monitor and blocks the thread; it does not allocate heap memory.

options.text: Because Java compiler syntax will fail with a compilation error if outside synchronized.
options.explanation: It compiles fine; the check is enforced at runtime throwing IllegalMonitorStateException.

options.text: To change the priority of the waiting thread to maximum.
options.explanation: Thread priority is unchanged by wait() or notify().

questions.body: Why should `wait()` always be invoked inside a `while` loop rather than an `if` statement?
questions.keyPoints: A while loop guards against spurious wakeups and ensures the predicate condition is re-evaluated before proceeding.

options.text: To guard against spurious wakeups and ensure the condition predicate still holds after the thread wakes up and reacquires the lock.
options.explanation: Threads can wake up without a notify (spurious wakeup), or another thread may consume the state condition before the waking thread reacquires the lock. Re-checking in a while loop is mandatory.

options.text: Because while loops run in kernel mode while if statements run in user mode.
options.explanation: Control flow statements execute identically in JVM bytecode.

options.text: Because an if statement releases the lock permanently, terminating the thread.
options.explanation: If statements do not alter lock lifecycle; wait() releases the monitor in both cases.

options.text: Because the Java bytecode verifier rejects wait() calls inside an if statement.
options.explanation: The bytecode verifier permits wait() inside any valid control structure.

questions.body: Which capability is provided by `java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock` that cannot be achieved with Java's standard `synchronized` keyword?
questions.keyPoints: ReentrantLock supports tryLock with timeout, lockInterruptibly, fairness policies, and multiple Condition instances.

options.text: Non-blocking timed lock acquisition (tryLock with timeout), interruptible lock attempts (lockInterruptibly), and configurable fairness policies.
options.explanation: ReentrantLock provides advanced features like tryLock(), lockInterruptibly(), fair lock ordering, and multiple Condition queues (newCondition()), which synchronized cannot do.

options.text: Allowing multiple threads to write concurrently without synchronization overhead.
options.explanation: ReentrantLock is an exclusive lock; it does not permit simultaneous concurrent writes.

options.text: Automatic lock release when an unhandled exception escapes, without needing a finally block.
options.explanation: ReentrantLock requires explicit release in a finally block; synchronized automatically releases when exiting its block.

options.text: Reentrancy for the same thread across nested methods.
options.explanation: Both synchronized and ReentrantLock are reentrant by the same thread.

questions.body: In what scenario does a `ReentrantReadWriteLock` provide a significant performance advantage over a standard `ReentrantLock`?
questions.keyPoints: ReentrantReadWriteLock allows multiple concurrent readers when writes are infrequent.

options.text: In read-heavy scenarios where data is read frequently by many concurrent threads but modified infrequently.
options.explanation: ReentrantReadWriteLock allows multiple reader threads to hold the read lock concurrently as long as no writer holds the write lock, boosting throughput for read-heavy workloads.

options.text: In write-heavy scenarios where hundreds of threads continuously modify shared state.
options.explanation: Under heavy writes, the lock contention and book-keeping overhead of ReadWriteLock make it slower than standard ReentrantLock.

options.text: When threads only need to communicate via message-passing channels.
options.explanation: Message channels use queues or actor mailboxes, not read-write locks.

options.text: When executing compute-bound tasks on single-core processors.
options.explanation: On single-core CPUs, concurrent read parallelization yields no hardware throughput advantage.

questions.body: Consider two threads: Thread A holds Lock 1 and requests Lock 2; Thread B holds Lock 2 and requests Lock 1. What technique is most effective at preventing this deadlock?
questions.keyPoints: Acquiring locks in a consistent, global order across all threads prevents cyclic wait deadlocks.

options.text: Enforce a strict, global lock acquisition ordering across all threads so every thread requests Lock 1 before Lock 2.
options.explanation: Deadlock requires a circular wait condition. Imposing a global linear order on lock acquisition breaks circular wait, making deadlocks impossible.

options.text: Increase thread priority of Thread A to preempt Thread B.
options.explanation: Thread priorities do not break lock ownership or eliminate circular wait conditions.

options.text: Set Thread.sleep(50) inside both critical sections to let the CPU yield.
options.explanation: Sleeping while holding a lock actually worsens deadlock likelihood and latency.

options.text: Replace both locks with non-volatile boolean flags.
options.explanation: Non-volatile flags are prone to visibility issues and race conditions.

questions.body: In a `ThreadPoolExecutor`, when a new task is submitted and the number of currently active threads is equal to `corePoolSize`, what is the executor's immediate next action?
questions.keyPoints: When corePoolSize threads are busy, submitted tasks are queued in the workQueue before creating additional threads up to maxPoolSize.

options.text: It attempts to enqueue the task into the blocking workQueue; only if the queue is full will it create a new thread up to maxPoolSize.
options.explanation: The standard ThreadPoolExecutor lifecycle: (1) if count < corePoolSize, spawn thread; (2) else offer task to workQueue; (3) if queue full and count < maxPoolSize, spawn thread; (4) else trigger RejectedExecutionHandler.

options.text: It immediately creates a new thread up to maxPoolSize before touching the queue.
options.explanation: Standard ThreadPoolExecutor only creates threads above corePoolSize if the work queue rejects/fails to accept the task.

options.text: It immediately rejects the task by throwing a RejectedExecutionException.
options.explanation: Rejection only happens when both the queue is full and active thread count has reached maxPoolSize.

options.text: It pauses the submitting thread until an existing core thread finishes its current task.
options.explanation: Submission does not pause unless a custom CallerRunsPolicy or bounded queue offer timeout is employed.

questions.body: Why is `Executors.newCachedThreadPool()` generally discouraged for high-throughput, latency-critical production backends?
questions.keyPoints: newCachedThreadPool has an unbounded maximum pool size (Integer.MAX_VALUE), which can cause OutOfMemoryError under sudden traffic spikes.

options.text: Its maximum pool size is unbounded (Integer.MAX_VALUE), which can exhaust OS threads, CPU context switching, and heap memory leading to OOM under load spikes.
options.explanation: newCachedThreadPool uses a SynchronousQueue with up to Integer.MAX_VALUE threads. Under heavy load, it creates an unbounded number of threads, exhausting system memory and thread handles.

options.text: It permanently caches submitted tasks in heap memory without ever executing them.
options.explanation: CachedThreadPool creates threads immediately to run tasks; it does not hoard unexecuted tasks.

options.text: It enforces single-threaded execution, creating a serialization bottleneck.
options.explanation: newSingleThreadExecutor is single-threaded; newCachedThreadPool scales up to unlimited threads.

options.text: It fails to clean up idle worker threads after inactivity.
options.explanation: It actively reclaims threads after 60 seconds of idle time; the issue is unbounded thread creation under peak load.

questions.body: What is the key functional difference between `CountDownLatch` and `CyclicBarrier`?
questions.keyPoints: CountDownLatch count cannot be reset once it reaches zero; CyclicBarrier can be reset and reused after all parties arrive.

options.text: CountDownLatch cannot be reset once its count reaches zero, whereas CyclicBarrier can be reset and reused across multiple iterative cycles.
options.explanation: CountDownLatch is a one-shot gate (countdown to 0). CyclicBarrier awaits a fixed number of threads (await()) and can be reused iteratively in cyclic computations.

options.text: CountDownLatch only works on a single CPU core, while CyclicBarrier leverages multi-socket architectures.
options.explanation: Both work uniformly across all CPU cores and sockets in the JVM.

options.text: CyclicBarrier terminates worker threads automatically when tripped, while CountDownLatch keeps them active.
options.explanation: Neither synchronization helper terminates worker threads.

options.text: CountDownLatch synchronizes threads across different JVM processes over TCP.
options.explanation: Both are intra-JVM in-memory synchronization constructs.

questions.body: In `CompletableFuture<T>`, what is the difference between `thenApply` and `thenCompose`?
questions.keyPoints: thenApply takes a function returning U (mapping T -> U); thenCompose takes a function returning CompletableFuture<U> (flatMapping, avoiding nested CompletableFuture).

options.text: thenApply transforms the result synchronously (T -> U) like map(), while thenCompose flattens another CompletableFuture (T -> CompletableFuture<U>) like flatMap().
options.explanation: thenApply(fn) returns CompletableFuture<U> where fn returns U. If fn returns CompletableFuture<U>, thenApply results in CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<U>>, whereas thenCompose flattens it to CompletableFuture<U>.

options.text: thenCompose executes only when an exception occurs, while thenApply executes only on success.
options.explanation: Exceptionally/handle handle errors; thenCompose chains successful async operations.

options.text: thenApply runs on a dedicated background thread pool, while thenCompose runs on the main thread.
options.explanation: Async variants (thenApplyAsync/thenComposeAsync) control thread pool execution.

options.text: thenCompose blocks the calling thread until all stages finish.
options.explanation: thenCompose is non-blocking and returns a new completion stage.

questions.body: How can using `ThreadLocal` in application servers that use thread pooling (such as Tomcat worker pools) cause memory leaks?
questions.keyPoints: ThreadLocal values in pooled threads persist if not explicitly removed with remove(), leaking class loaders and context objects.

options.text: Pooled threads are kept alive indefinitely; if ThreadLocal.remove() is not called in a finally block, references remain retained in Thread.threadLocals.
options.explanation: Since pool threads do not terminate between HTTP requests, entries in their ThreadLocalMap retain references to request data and webapp ClassLoaders, causing severe memory leaks unless explicitly cleaned via remove().

options.text: ThreadLocal variables prevent the JVM Metaspace from loading new classes.
options.explanation: They do not halt class loading; they prevent classloaders and loaded classes from being unloaded from Metaspace/heap upon redeployment.

options.text: ThreadLocal bypasses garbage collection by allocating memory in OS swap space.
options.explanation: ThreadLocal instances and values reside in the standard JVM heap.

options.text: ThreadLocal forces all threads to serialize writes to a single shared synchronized map.
options.explanation: ThreadLocal is per-thread storage, not a single shared synchronized map.

questions.body: How does the work-stealing algorithm in `ForkJoinPool` optimize throughput for divide-and-conquer parallel tasks?
questions.keyPoints: Idle worker threads steal tasks from the tail/deques of busy worker threads to balance load and minimize contention.

options.text: Each worker thread has its own double-ended queue (deque); idle threads steal tasks from the opposite end (tail) of busy threads' deques to minimize contention.
options.explanation: Worker threads push and pop tasks from their own deque head (LIFO for cache locality), while idle threads steal tasks from the tail (FIFO) of other workers' deques, minimizing lock contention.

options.text: Idle threads pause busy threads and force them to migrate their CPU registers.
options.explanation: Work-stealing operates cooperatively at the task queue level, not via CPU register interruption.

options.text: It shares a single global concurrent queue protected by a fair spinlock.
options.explanation: A single shared queue creates massive contention; ForkJoinPool uses per-worker deques precisely to avoid this.

options.text: It executes subtasks recursively on the operating system kernel dispatch queue.
options.explanation: ForkJoinPool executes tasks entirely in user-space worker threads.

questions.body: What is 'false sharing' in multi-threaded Java applications, and how does the JVM address it?
questions.keyPoints: False sharing occurs when independent variables reside on the same CPU cache line (64 bytes), causing invalidation traffic across cores; @Contended adds padding.

options.text: Independent variables updated by different threads reside on the same CPU cache line (typically 64 bytes), triggering costly cache invalidations across cores; @Contended adds cache padding.
options.explanation: When two threads write to distinct variables that reside on the same 64-byte L1/L2 cache line, cache coherency protocols (MESI) invalidate the entire cache line across CPU cores. The @Contended annotation inserts padding to isolate variables onto distinct cache lines.

options.text: Two threads share an encryption key without performing a Diffie-Hellman handshake.
options.explanation: False sharing is a CPU hardware cache performance phenomenon, not a cryptographic handshake issue.

options.text: A race condition where two threads acquire the same non-reentrant mutex simultaneously.
options.explanation: This describes mutual exclusion failure, not false sharing.

options.text: Multiple JVM processes sharing a single memory page in Linux virtual memory.
options.explanation: Shared memory pages across processes is OS inter-process memory sharing, not CPU cache-line bouncing.

questions.body: How does `StampedLock` support optimistic reading in Java 8+, and why does it outperform `ReentrantReadWriteLock`?
questions.keyPoints: tryOptimisticRead returns a stamp without acquiring an exclusive lock; validate(stamp) checks if a write occurred, avoiding cache line invalidation from reader lock tracking.

options.text: It issues an optimistic stamp without locking; if validate(stamp) confirms no write intervened, the read completes with zero lock contention and no state mutation.
options.explanation: tryOptimisticRead() does not increment reader counts or acquire locks, avoiding CPU cache invalidation. The reader validates the stamp afterwards; if invalid, it falls back to a pessimistic read lock.

options.text: It duplicates the entire object graph in thread memory before every read operation.
options.explanation: It does not clone or duplicate heap objects; it validates state consistency via stamps.

options.text: It is reentrant, allowing nested calls without any deadlock risk under any circumstance.
options.explanation: StampedLock is explicitly NOT reentrant; acquiring it reentrantly will cause self-deadlock.

options.text: It replaces all locks with non-blocking software transactional memory (STM).
options.explanation: Java does not implement general STM; StampedLock uses ticket/version-based validation.

questions.body: Introduced in Java 21, what is the primary architectural difference between Virtual Threads and traditional Platform Threads?
questions.keyPoints: Virtual threads are lightweight, user-mode threads managed by the JVM that unmount from carrier threads when blocking, enabling millions of concurrent threads.

options.text: Virtual threads are lightweight JVM-managed threads that unmount from OS carrier threads during blocking I/O, allowing millions of concurrent tasks with minimal memory footprint.
options.explanation: Unlike platform threads (1:1 with OS threads consuming ~1MB stack), virtual threads (M:N scheduling) are JVM heap objects with small initial stacks. When blocking on I/O, they unmount from carrier threads, freeing OS threads for other work.

options.text: Virtual threads run CPU-bound numeric calculations 10x faster than platform threads by bypassing bytecode interpretation.
options.explanation: Virtual threads do not speed up CPU-bound computation; they enhance throughput and scalability for high-concurrency blocking I/O.

options.text: Virtual threads disable thread synchronization and locks completely to avoid deadlocks.
options.explanation: Virtual threads support standard synchronization and locks; pinning can occur if holding synchronized blocks during blocking I/O.

options.text: Virtual threads run exclusively on GPU hardware cores rather than the CPU.
options.explanation: Virtual threads are scheduled on standard CPU carrier threads in a ForkJoinPool.

questions.body: Under extremely high write contention from dozens of threads, why is `LongAdder` significantly faster than `AtomicLong`?
questions.keyPoints: LongAdder maintains an internal array of Cell counters that threads update independently, reducing CAS contention on a single variable, and sums them when needed.

options.text: LongAdder distributes updates across a dynamically sized array of Cells to minimize CAS contention across threads, summing them only when sum() is queried.
options.explanation: AtomicLong spins on CAS against a single memory location, causing heavy CPU bus contention under load. LongAdder stripes mutations across Cell objects hashed by thread, combining them on read.

options.text: LongAdder executes in GPU compute shaders rather than main memory.
options.explanation: LongAdder runs entirely in standard JVM heap memory.

options.text: LongAdder uses optimistic locking without ever performing atomic operations.
options.explanation: LongAdder uses CAS operations on individual Cell counters in the cell array.

options.text: LongAdder buffers updates to an asynchronous disk log before committing.
options.explanation: LongAdder is an in-memory accumulator; no disk I/O is involved.
